Getting Started > Erlang Concurrency Candidates and a Verse Transaction Survey
Status: evaluation record (2026-10-29); the current state of the Erlang surface was synced on 2026-10-30. This page registers the evaluation conclusions and Jev rulings for the Erlang concurrency candidates and the Verse transaction survey; implementation scheduling follows the ordering chain in Section 9 of Document 13 and Document 15. Current state: the supervision structure and monitor have landed with Ordering One and been integrated and closed (2026-10-30, sci main e7c18568 / sa_plugin_sla master 6004af4, see Sections 1 and 5); the home of the OTP skeleton has been ruled to be .sla idioms in sci's sa_std, landing with Ordering Two; budget-based yielding remains a registered goroutine v2 item. Verse / STM still belongs to Ordering Three and has not been touched.

1. Erlang Candidates (main-session evaluation)

Erlang's strength is the fault architecture on the BEAM virtual machine: the Actor model with zero shared state, true preemptive scheduling budgeted by reduction counts, and a fault-tolerance system made of links/monitors plus supervision trees, along with distribution and hot upgrades. Its processes are first of all fault-isolation domains; parallelism is only a by-product. Four candidates are taken from it:

  • Promote the supervision structure to a first-class std component: on top of the goroutine-boundary recover already adopted in Document 15, turn restart strategies into declarative std components (a group of goroutines hangs under a supervisor, with one-for-one / restart-the-whole-group / a restart-intensity cap written out), instead of every server hand-writing its own recover loop. — Landed (2026-10-30): the first-class std component sa_std/supervisor.sla (supervise / supervise_policy, one-for-one + a restart budget) and the go supervised boundary spawn were integrated and closed with the syntax batch; for a usage example, see Example 5 in Section 15 of Document 13.
  • monitor: death notification as a message: when a goroutine exits or crashes, deliver to the monitoring party a signal that can be received via a channel / select, turning “waiting for the other party to die” from polling into an event. On the runtime side it is only a small primitive, and it fits the already-decided channel + select surface seamlessly. — Landed (2026-10-30): monitor(handle) returns a Chan<(u64, i32)>; both normal exit and a boundary trap are delivered as (handle, code) messages and can be received via select, and the trap record can additionally be read back via sa_task_trap_info; the runtime primitive landed with the sci companion. For a usage example, see Example 6 in Section 15 of Document 13.
  • Budget-based yield checks: a static version of Erlang's reduction counting — the compiler inserts counting checks at loop back-edges / call sites, and yields when the budget is exhausted. This is the proper cure for “a CPU-bound goroutine that never yields starves its companions”, but it requires changing compiler emission, so it is registered as a goroutine phase-two candidate. — Not landed: it remains the headline registered item for goroutine v2 and was not touched in this batch.
  • The OTP-style server skeleton as a std library idiom: a gen_server-shaped standard server skeleton (init / handle / state loop) is a pure library-layer pattern; once the syntax batch lands, make it an SLA std idiom without touching the language. — Not landed; its landing place has been ruled: a Jev ruling (2026-10-30, in preparation for Ordering Two) places it in sci's sa_std as an .sla idiom file + tests (sa_std_idiom 1.0), to land together with the Ordering Two goroutine rework of the three machines.

Three items not taken: the full mailbox + selective-receive set (single-queue pattern-matching receive semantics are complex and its scanning cost is notorious; channels + select already cover the main value and the ownership story is cleaner); immutable + copy semantics (the exact opposite of ownership zero-copy — on “no sharing” we take the statically stronger road of passing ownership over channels and do not switch roads); distribution and hot upgrades (all three machines are single-machine comparison targets, and db explicitly refuses a network-listening surface, so this is unrelated to this ecosystem).

Isolation comparison: an Erlang process's isolation is bought with “per-process GC + copy everything”, which is exactly what a no-GC model cannot afford and need not pay for — our supervision goes through boundary traps + the ownership stack; the isolation strength is enough for servers, at an order of magnitude lower cost.

2. Verse Survey Conclusions (in-depth research, 2026-10-29)

Verse is Epic's language for UEFN / UE6: conceived by Tim Sweeney, designed by Simon Peyton Jones and others, first released with UEFN in March 2023; in June 2026, State of Unreal announced it as the foundation language of UE6, with UE6 early access set for the end of 2027.

Lineage correction: Verse has no Erlang ancestry. Its roots are in Haskell's STM (software transactional memory) and logic programming — its core calculus is in The Verse Calculus. Erlang (zero sharing + message passing) and Verse (shared state + transactions) are two opposite answers to “why is concurrency hard”, not relatives.

What has shipped: first, local failure-rollback transactions — a Verse expression can “fail” (no value, not an exception); writes to a var inside a failure context are tentative, committed only if the context as a whole succeeds, and rolled back as a whole if any step fails; its runtime, AutoRTFM, is a write-log-style single-threaded transaction system, already running in production on Fortnite servers. Second, function-signature effect annotations: <transacts> (may change state rollback-ably), <decides> (may fail), <suspends> (asynchronous), <varies> and the like are written into signatures and statically checked by the compiler, and non-rollback-able functions are by default forbidden from entering a failure context.

What has not shipped (announced / design goals): parallel STM — Sweeney publicly named Haskell's Composable Memory Transactions as the blueprint (many updates executing speculatively in parallel, committing when there is no conflict, retrying on conflict); client prediction — seen only in an unpublished <predicts> effect design in the Book of Verse (the client runs a prediction, the server corrects authoritatively). Both are UE6 goals, not ready-made mechanisms.

Verse's concurrency core is cooperative coroutines: race / sync / rush / branch and spawn; and <suspends> and <decides> cannot coexist in one body — there is a hard seam between the asynchronous world and the transactional world.

3. Main-Session Evaluation: Where the Three-Way Comparison Converges

Where our concurrency choice sits on the spectrum: the main body stands on the Erlang side (goroutine isolation + channels + supervision), while transactions exist only at the db engine layer as explicit write sets (write-set staging + atomic commit) — that is, each side contributes the half that suits a no-GC + ownership model.

  • Verse's most actionable value is its effect annotations: it proved at Epic scale that “writing suspends / transacts / decides into function signatures, enforced by the compiler” is feasible. That is exactly the proper form of a solution to the function-coloring problem — not eliminating the coloring, but turning the coloring into a checkable contract. It speaks directly to the “async interoperability stance” item already listed for the SLA syntax batch: spawn, channel operations, and capabilities that may trap should be visible in signatures and checked.
  • Verse-style implicit rollback is not adopted: the implicit semantics of “write first and ask later; failure automatically undoes it” clashes with our explicit discipline, and none of the three machines does speculative execution, so there is no consumption scenario; where we need transactions (db) we already have our own version, the explicit write set.
  • Online prediction / rollback is not adopted (observation only): that is a proposition of game netcode (multiplayer online state prediction and reconciliation); no such species exists among our deliverables, and the mechanism itself has not been released on Epic's side either.

  • monitor death notification (via channel / select): adopted, 0.81. (Landed; see Section 1.)
  • OTP-style server skeleton as a std idiom: adopted, 0.77. (Not landed; its home has been ruled to be an .sla idiom in sci's sa_std, with Ordering Two.)
  • Budget-based yield checks: registered as the goroutine v2 headline, 0.74. (Not landed.)
  • Supervision structure as a first-class std component: adopted with the SLA syntax batch, 0.72. (Landed with the syntax batch.)
  • Verse-style effect annotations: into the async interoperability design of the SLA syntax batch, 0.66. (Landed with the syntax batch in the form of effect rule R2; see Sections 11 and 14 of Document 13.)
  • Reserve the runtime half of monitor in runtime v1: 0.58 (mildly positive — keep the shape without expanding acceptance). (Runtime v1 delivered that surface, and the syntax-batch companion completed the consumption semantics.)
  • Verse implicit transaction rollback not adopted: confirmed, 0.86.
  • Online prediction / parallel STM observation only: confirmed, 0.86.

5. Status and Scheduling

This page is the registry for the Erlang / Verse candidate routes and their evaluations. Current state (2026-10-30): the main body of the Erlang surface has landed and been integrated and closed — runtime phase one (sci 870cda60) delivered goroutine boundary traps / recover, monitor delivery and the supervision primitives, and context cancellation's Done channel; the SLA syntax batch (sa_plugin_sla 6004af4 + sci companion e7c18568) delivered go supervised, the monitor syntax surface, the supervisor.sla first-class std component, and the Verse-style effect rule R2; the closing account is in Section 14 of Document 13 and usage examples in its Section 15. Two items have not landed: the OTP skeleton (home = an .sla idiom file in sci's sa_std; Jev ruled sa_std_idiom 1.0 on 2026-10-30; it lands with the Ordering Two goroutine rework of the three machines); budget-based yielding (the goroutine v2 headline, still registered). Verse implicit rollback and online prediction are not proposed as projects; the narrow STM form still belongs to Ordering Three and has not passed its two gates (see Section 6).

6. The Narrow STM Candidate (Haskell explicit style, 2026-10-29)

The distinction first: the STM in this section means the Haskell explicit style — an atomically block delimits the scope, reads and writes go through transactional variables, conflicts retry automatically, and blocks compose (including orElse's “try A, and if that fails try B”). It is not the same thing as the Verse implicit rollback described in Section 2 and rejected in Section 4 (writing into a failure context is automatically tentative / undone; non-adoption confirmed at 0.86) — rejecting the implicit style does not mean rejecting the explicit style, so this section is ruled separately.

Main-session evaluation points:

  • STM's real skill is composability: atomically can nest and merge, and orElse provides coordination composition — something neither locks nor channels can give; at the theory level it is not condemned to death.
  • The tension is that it presupposes multi-party shared mutable state, which clashes with our ownership discipline: the answer queue for shared state already has an order — the owner-goroutine pattern (the OTP skeleton) → Mutex / RwLock (already included in runtime phase one's Period C) → the db engine layer; STM can only queue behind that line.
  • Its applicable surface is limited: retry storms under hot-key conflicts, and the ban on doing I/O inside a transaction (nothing may be persisted until after commit) limit its use on large state; Clojure's STM is likewise used only for small-to-medium coordination state, not as a database engine — the narrow form is delimited at exactly that scale.
  • The checker is the roadblock: that a transaction may retry means the code in the block may execute multiple times — side effects must be statically banned (I/O and channel operations must not enter the block); and the ownership of owned values inside a transaction unit along the read / write / rollback / retry paths must be decidable. This is research-grade checker design, not something a syntax batch can carry along. A feasible leverage path is Verse's effect annotations: use signature effects to delimit rollback-able code, connecting to the effect-annotation line already adopted in Section 4 (0.66).

Jev ruling (2026-10-29, jev-1.14.0, ruling file ~/workspace/jev-designs/stm_narrow_candidate.json): the narrow form — explicit atomically + restricted transaction units, serving only small goroutine coordination state, queued after goroutine v2, with a checker-feasibility census before any project is proposed — is registered as a long-term candidate at 0.63 (mildly positive). But both gates currently run cold: the demand gate, 0.30 (after the three machines are reworked with the owner pattern + locks, the expectation that profiling can really reveal a coordination pain point that “only STM can solve” is low); the checker-feasibility gate, 0.36 (extending a transactional discipline without endangering the soundness of the existing Referee machinery has a weak grip and is research-grade risk).

Adoption disposition (default agreement): register it as a long-term candidate under a two-gate system — if either the demand gate (profiling evidence after the three-machine rework) or the feasibility gate (a checker census) fails, it closes; it does not enter the current SLA syntax batch and does not move the three-machine rework plan.

7. Overall Positioning, Wrapped Up (set by the user on 2026-10-29)

The must-build main line (the load-bearing wall): Go's execution model as the base (goroutines + channels / select + sync + defer) × Erlang's fault architecture over the top (boundary recover, the supervision structure, monitor death notification, the context cancellation convention) × effect annotations stolen from Verse as the contract layer — this is the concurrency foundation of the three machines and CXU; it is under construction / scheduled, with no room for negotiation.

STM is the spare-parts cabinet: it does not even count as a second pillar. Only when the main line's own tools (owner goroutines, Mutex / RwLock, db's explicit write-set transactions) are proven by profiling to be insufficient at some specific coordination point, and the checker-feasibility census passes (the two gates, see Section 6), may it be enabled in narrow form; most likely it will never be used, but its theoretical place is reserved.

In one sentence: the goroutine complex is the load-bearing wall; STM is the spare-parts cabinet.
